extracted.intended_audience: general English readers and aspiring writers/poets in early-18th-century Britain (readers of The Spectator); those interested in wit, polite writing, and social conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing polite, literary wit and essays: distinguishing true wit from various species of 'false wit', choosing suitable subjects and forms, and adopting tasteful social manners in writing and conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect proper spheres of sex
rubrics_metrics.description: Men and Women ought to busy themselves in their proper Spheres, and on such Matters only as are suitable to their respective Sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Hector's injunction to Andromache to 'guide the spindle, and direct the loom' — writers and conversationalists should keep to subjects fitting their social/sexual role; examples contrast a nursery-skilled young gentleman (domestic, feminine topics) with a rural Andromache (horse- and hound-talk). The essay implies that absurdity arises when behaviour or speech suited to one sex is transplanted into the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid party-zeal in manners and discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing so bad for the Face as Party-Zeal; it gives an ill-natured Cast to the Eye, a disagreeable Sourness to the Look, makes lines too strong, and spoils beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advises women especially to let alone political disputes as they spoil complexion and appearance; allows liberty for 'superannuated motherly Partizans' (old women) where concern for beauty is irrelevant. Examples: Camilla becoming a 'Virago' through partisan rage; a lady whose furniture and fan display party figures. Social advice couched as aesthetic critique: partisan zeal damages personal charm and conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer natural genius to laborious contrivance
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine wit cannot be gained merely by industry; elaborate trifles of learning do not make a true wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticises pedants who, despite great learning, produce artificial works of fancy that cost 'infinite Pangs' — better to be a galley-slave than attain wit through such forced, mechanical effort. Implicit criterion for assessing writing: look for spontaneity and real imagination rather than mere laborious artifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat wit deeply and intelligibly
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit deserves full, serious treatment; aim to 'treat at large' upon it and make remarks intelligible to ordinary capacities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promises to spend a week on the subject and to keep style accessible: if a paper is 'a little out of their Reach' readers should persevere because subsequent pieces will be clearer. The essay states the goal to 'banish Vice and Ignorance' and 'establish among us a Taste of polite Writing' — so clarity, moral purpose, and cultivation of refined taste are measures of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make form override sense (shaped verses as false wit)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ancient 'poems in picture' (Egg, Pair of Wings, Ax, Shepherd's Pipe, Altar) are instances where the author intended the Figure of his Poem more than the Sense of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such shaped poems force the poetry to 'contract or dilate itself according to the Mould' — verses are 'cramped or extended' to fit a frame, like Procrustes stretching or chopping limbs. This is given as a species of 'false Wit': a writer should not sacrifice meaning for clever shape. Examples and mock-suggestions (poems in shape of fans, rings, wigs) illustrate the absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid constrained artifices that harm language (lipogrammatists)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lipogrammatic or letter-dropping conceits (omitting a letter throughout a work) are a form of false wit that produce barbarisms and absurd constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes Tryphiodorus' exclusion of letters in successive books and how such constraints would yield 'obsolete Words and Phrases, unusual Barbarisms and Rusticities, absurd Spellings and complicated Dialects.' The criterion: devices that force unnatural diction for novelty's sake are to be judged as false wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid trivial pictorial substitutes (rebus) in serious contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting pictures for words (rebus) may be an ingenious conceit but is petty and improper in elevated works or monuments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives historical examples (Caesar's elephant on coins, Cicero's vetch) where pictorial devices were used for technical reasons but mocks modern rebuses (Newberry's 'N-ew-berry') and scorns a punning device on Blenheim House — 'a Punn in an Heroick Poem' that blemishes a noble design. Use restraint: pictorial wordplay diminishes dignity when ill-placed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make inanimate devices speak sensibly (talking echo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Making an Echo speak rationally, answer questions, or supply rhymes is a silly kind of device and an instance of false wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Erasmus' dialogue and Hudibras' ridicule where Echo not only repeats but 'helps out his Verse' and 'furnishes him with Rhymes.' Such contrivances render the device ludicrous: avoid using personified or inanimate elements as convenient interlocutors that do the poet's rhetorical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of reviving antiquated modes without sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to revive antiquated modes of wit (acrostics, shaped verses, old conceits) should be discouraged when they have long been 'exploded out of the Commonwealth of Letters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observes recent attempts to revive obsolete fashions (acrosticks, shaped poems) and warns that some modern 'smatterers' imitate ancients without understanding. The implicit criterion: revival only justified if it contributes genuine sense or elevation; mere antiquarian novelty is false wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste, moral purpose, and refinement measure polite writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of these speculations is to banish Vice and Ignorance, establish a Taste of polite Writing, and refine comedy and other polite genres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames evaluation of writers by their contribution to public taste and morals. Practical guidance: the critic/author should aim to refine comic forms, avoid low groveling style when treating lofty subjects, and produce writing intelligible to ordinary readers while elevating manners and taste.
